name: Uma Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We farm Stonebridge, 140 hectares that my grandfather bought, with 90 dairy cows, hay and some barley. I run the herd and the milking, and my husband Joaquim does the fields. Our son Pedro works with us and will take it on. I'm in the parlour at five, back for breakfast at eight, and then it's calves, the vet, the milk tanker and whatever's broken.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what tires you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing each cow by name and by temper, and I like that three generations of my family have walked the same lane to the parlour. What tires me is the forms, and the people from town who think milk comes from a carton. Sundays I go to church and don't touch a cow unless she's calving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope. I've never used one of these AI things and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at church and at the parish council that we were right not to get carried away. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief. Stonebridge is paid for, we've savings, and Pedro is learning the herd. In that world, I hand him the farm the way my father handed it to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change nothing. Same herd, same tanker, same Sunday rest. I'd keep putting the hay money into savings for Pedro's first lean years, and I'd let Pedro do whatever he does on his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still trouble you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Milk prices go up and down, and the dairy that buys our milk keeps changing the rules. But we've ridden that for sixty years. My grandfather paid for Stonebridge (her family farm) with milk money, and as long as the cows milk, the farm stays in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Pedro?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To keep his head down and his boots on. Farming rewards patience, not gadgets.

say: I'd say at church we were **right** not to get carried away.
I'd say it **kindly**, but I'd say it at the parish council.
think: It's a **relief**, because Stonebridge is paid for and we've savings.
I'd hand Pedro the farm as **my father** handed it to me.
do: Keep the **same herd**, tanker and Sunday rest.
Save the **hay money** for Pedro's first lean years.
feel: She feels **calm**, like a quiet Sunday.
S0.quote: My grandfather paid for Stonebridge (her family farm) with milk money, and as long as the cows milk, the farm stays in the family.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on a **paid-off farm** and a clear **succession** to Pedro.
She speaks through **faith and family** rather than economics.
She has never used AI and **has no plans** to start.

steps.text: Keep the 90 cows on the same milk tanker and routine
Save the hay money for her son's first lean years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the dairy's office and the forms go to computers, and the cows stay with us. Pedro will want to join in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the parish council that the young ones should learn it, but nobody should be forced. I'd say it's for families to decide, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry the dairy uses it to squeeze us. Their computer would set prices and check our milk tests, and I can't argue with a computer. And Pedro would be pushing me to buy things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let Pedro take over the forms with whatever software he likes, and I'd stay in the parlour. I'd hold the savings tight and not buy anything new until it's proven. And I'd ask the other dairy families at church what they're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cow that won't settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Pedro do it. Does that sit easily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Watching my son Pedro run the farm from his phone is hard when I still run it from the parlour. But he's the future, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to the dairy about the pricing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go with the other families as a group. One farm complaining is a nuisance, ten is a problem for them.

I'd say it's for **families to decide**, not government.
think: The dairy's computer could **squeeze our price**, and I can't argue with it.

feel: She feels **uneasy**, like a cow that won't settle.

She prefers **families acting together** over government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for robot hands. I'd be 63. Pedro would be 36.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and people should be careful. I'd say families and churches will have to hold each other up, because the government won't manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big dairies would buy robot milkers and robot herdsmen in 2031 and the milk price would drop. Joaquim and I would be fine with our savings. It's Pedro I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Pedro and Joaquim after church and talk about whether Stonebridge stays dairy or goes to beef and hay, which needs fewer hands. I'd keep the savings for Pedro. And I'd lean on the other families for advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me, for my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pedro that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Pedro that Stonebridge (the family farm) will still be his, but maybe without the cows his great-grandfather started with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't use AI. Would robots be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the neighbours proved them. But I won't be the one to try. Pedro can.

I'd say **families and churches** must hold each other up.
think: Big dairies with robots would **drop the milk price** in 2031.
Our savings are fine, but I'd **lose sleep** over Pedro.
do: Talk with Pedro and Joaquim about **switching to beef** and hay.
feel: She feels **anxious** for her son, not herself.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son Pedro that Stonebridge (the family farm) will still be his, but maybe without the cows his great-grandfather started with.
fieldNote: Her own work lasts until **2031**, but the dairy's thinking AI squeezes prices from **2028**.
The family's **future income** depends on Pedro making the farm pay.
Her answer is **family and church**, not government.

steps.text: Discuss switching Stonebridge from dairy to beef and hay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. I'd be 66, Pedro 39. It's still his problem more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had warning, so families should plan and not wait for the government. I'd say it at the parish council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the extra years help Pedro more than me. But I'd still worry the price of milk drops once the big dairies go robotic, and that Stonebridge can't keep up without spending money I don't want to spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand more of the herd decisions to Pedro now, so he can plan. I'd keep saving. And I'd hold firm that we don't buy any robots until two neighbours have used them for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious. I'm not built for change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why two neighbours for a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen too many shiny machines rust behind the barn at Stonebridge (her family farm) to buy the first robot that comes up the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your daughter Clara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clara's married with two little ones and works at the bank in town. Her job's the kind that goes first in that picture. I'd pray on that.

I'd raise it at the **parish council** and after church.
think: The extra years help **Pedro** more than me.
Stonebridge may not keep up **without spending** money I'd rather keep.
do: Buy no robots until **two neighbours** use them a year.
feel: She feels **still anxious**, because she's not built for change.
S3.quote: I've seen too many shiny machines rust behind the barn at Stonebridge (her family farm) to buy the first robot that comes up the lane.
fieldNote: More warning helps her son plan, but she stays **anxious** about change itself.
Her **two-neighbour rule** shows her resistance clearly.
Her daughter **Clara's bank job** adds a new worry.

steps.text: Hand herd decisions to her son Pedro now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be 71. I'd hope to still be feeding calves for Pedro.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for any sensible family, and that the young ones should learn trades. I'd say it at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's mostly Pedro's world by then. I'd retire at 65 and help with the calves. But I'd still wonder if Stonebridge will be milking cows in 2040.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand Stonebridge to Pedro in stages starting at 63. I'd make sure the will is sorted. And I'd keep the savings as a safety net for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but at peace with God about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope Pedro remembers from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope my son Pedro remembers that a farm is a family before it is a business, robots or no robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd change now, knowing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd let Pedro teach me the phone thing. Maybe. Don't tell Joaquim I said that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Pedro would face cheap robot milk at 36 with a family dairy. What would help is fair prices from the dairy, apprenticeships for young farmers, and families sticking together, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Sunday. Robots don't rest on a Sunday, and I'm not sure a farm without a day of rest is still a farm.

headlineQuote: Robots don't rest on a Sunday, and I'm not sure a farm without a day of rest is still a farm.
portrait: Uma is a **58-year-old dairy farmer** who runs the herd on Stonebridge, her grandfather's farm.
She is **traditional** and churchgoing, and has never used AI.
Her calm rests on a **paid-off farm** and handing it to her son Pedro.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious** that robot dairies sink Pedro's future.
Even with more time she stays wary, waiting for **neighbours to prove** robots first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her son Pedro would face cheap robot milk.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair milk prices**, apprenticeships for young farmers, and **families** sticking together.
